solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping); the post gives the 23ac/13ac/2dn group as 'SING ONE PRAISES' (14 letters) but the grid's own (4,4,7) enumeration and 13ac's 4-letter slot need 'ONES', matching the idiom 'sing one's praises' -- read as SING ONES PRAISES (15 letters)

clue.text: Having got an erection, don't let go of support

blocks.note: something erected has been put up, so it is up
to keep hold of something is not to let go

explanation.surface: A smutty Private Eye joke about clinging on once aroused.
explanation.walkthrough: The innuendo is the disguise: the erection simply means something raised, and 'don't let go' is an instruction to grip.
explanation.definitionFit: To uphold a cause or a decision is to back it and keep it standing, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: see 23ac.
Voting Brexit? Git not up to timeless reforms

indicators.note: time is abbreviated T, and being without time means that letter is dropped
to reform something is to reshape it, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the word 'to' with its T removed

explanation.surface: Someone sneers that an idiot is not ready for the reforms that leaving the EU would bring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Git' is a British insult for an annoying person. The 'to' loses its T before joining the anagram fodder; the question mark flags the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Voting to leave the European Union is an instance of choosing to withdraw from a membership arrangement, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Hell meets Conservative circle music genre!

blocks.note: Dis is the classical underworld, another name for hell
C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative
a circle is shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A hellish evening where a Tory social circle discovers a new style of music.
explanation.walkthrough: Dis was the Roman god of the underworld, so the name stands for hell; the circle is the round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Disco is the dance-oriented style of popular music that flourished in the 1970s, an example of a genre.

clue.text: Ex-driver's sound boost

indicators.note: the sound of a name rather than its spelling is what is wanted

blocks.note: Prince Philip gave up his driving licence in 2019 after a car crash

explanation.surface: A retired motorist's voice is given a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: The ex-driver is Prince Philip, the Queen's husband, who surrendered his licence aged 97 after crashing near Sandringham in 2019.
explanation.definitionFit: A fillip is a stimulus or encouragement that gives something a lift, so it works as a noun synonym.

clue.text: Put to rest with Jack, etc, possibly ejaculate

indicators.note: 'possibly' allows that the letters may come in some other order

blocks.note: to inter is to bury, laying a body to rest
J is the abbreviation for jack in a pack of cards
taken as written

explanation.surface: A burial for a man called Jack, with a crude closing word in true Private Eye style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ejaculate' is used in its old literary sense of exclaiming suddenly, which the surface deliberately smuttifies.
explanation.definitionFit: In older writing, to ejaculate means to blurt out a remark, which is to cut in with a sudden exclamation.

clue.text: Nothing's going up – try tongue

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: nil means nothing, a zero score
to have a go is to have a try

explanation.surface: Nothing is happening, so have a go at using your tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' means a language here, not the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingo is an informal word for a language or dialect, and tongue is the old word for a language.

clue.text: Groom penetrated by alien before adolescence

indicators.note: something penetrated has another thing pushed inside it

blocks.note: to preen is to groom oneself
ET is the alien of the Spielberg film

explanation.surface: A lurid tabloid headline about a bridegroom and an extraterrestrial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' reads as a noun (a bridegroom) but is the verb for tidying oneself up.
explanation.definitionFit: A pre-teen child is one aged just under thirteen, so not yet in the teenage years of puberty.

clue.text: Derisive press in command

blocks.note: to iron clothes is to press them
IC is the abbreviation for in charge or in command

explanation.surface: A sneering newspaper that is running the show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' looks like the newspapers but is the verb for ironing.
explanation.definitionFit: An ironic remark says the opposite of what is meant, often to mock, so it is scornful or derisive in tone.

clue.text: (& 16ac.) Gen. Halting's very time-consuming task when it comes to Trump's tweets etc?

definitions.text: very time-consuming task when it comes to Trump's tweets etc?

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information or the facts, and a single fact is a piece of it
checking an advance is halting it

explanation.surface: A general called Halting faces an exhausting job verifying the US president's social media posts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gen. Halting' reads as an army officer's name, but 'gen' is British slang for information and 'halting' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Verifying claims made by Donald Trump on Twitter was notoriously laborious for journalists, so the whole phrase describes that work.

clue.text: Rest cure organised to accommodate elected poll-watcher?

indicators.note: things that are organised have been put into a fresh order
to accommodate a guest is to give them room inside

blocks.note: taken as written
a candidate who is elected is in

explanation.surface: A tired election official is prescribed a spell of recuperation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elected' gives IN, as in a party being in power.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrutineer is an official who oversees the counting of votes at an election, so a watcher of the poll.

clue.text: Tabloid on depression: "here's a timely drink"

indicators.note: one thing set on another sits beside it in sequence, the first leading

blocks.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
a downer is a gloomy mood or depressing experience

explanation.surface: A tabloid feature on depression recommends a drink at just the right moment.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is Britain's best-known red-top tabloid; 'timely' fits because the drink is defined by the hour it is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: A sundowner is an alcoholic drink taken at sunset, so it is a drink tied to a particular time of day.

clue.text: see 23ac.
Like topless hooker getting off the boat

indicators.note: without a top means the first letter is lost

blocks.note: as means like, in comparisons
a hooker is slang for a prostitute

explanation.surface: A semi-naked prostitute stepping onto the quay from a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' is not about clothing: it beheads the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To be ashore is to be on land rather than at sea, which is where you are once you have disembarked.

clue.text: Pathetically puerile and, oh, not Rees-Mogg?

indicators.note: something done pathetically is botched, leaving the letters in a mess

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Mocking the Brexiteer Jacob Rees-Mogg as childish and feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacob Rees-Mogg is a prominent Conservative Brexit campaigner, so the definition works by describing his opposite, signalled by the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Rees-Mogg is a famous Eurosceptic, so someone unlike him is an enthusiast for the European Union.

clue.text: see 10ac.
Where chopper might well be made use of by Brenda ? Lord!

blocks.clueFragment: Where chopper might well be made use of
blocks.note: a chopper is a cleaver, a tool used in the room where food is prepared
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, and ER stands for Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Imagining the Queen wielding a cleaver, or something ruder, with an exclamation of shock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chopper' invites a vulgar reading, but it is a kitchen knife. Lord Kitchener was the British war secretary on the famous 'Your Country Needs You' poster.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbert Kitchener was made an earl, so he is an example of a peer known by his title, Lord Kitchener.

clue.text: Loose corset that is contracted and concealed

indicators.note: loose things are not held in place, so the letters slip into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
i.e. is the shortened form of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A slack undergarment that has been tightened and hidden from view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contracted' suggests tightening the corset, but it means abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoteric knowledge is reserved for an inner circle of initiates, so it is hidden or secret from outsiders.

clue.text: Put your foot in it, introducing Republican to liberal purist

definitions.note: phrased as an instruction; the answer is the thing the foot goes in

indicators.note: to introduce something is to bring it in, so a letter goes inside
a liberal approach is free and loose, so the letters are not kept in order

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: Making a gaffe by bringing a right-winger to meet a strict liberal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put your foot in it' looks like the idiom for blundering, but read literally it describes what a rider does with the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A stirrup is the loop hanging from a saddle into which a horse rider places a boot, so it is literally what the foot goes in.

clue.text: Informal, anti-Trump state holding America up

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside your grasp
in a down entry, up means read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: California, a Democratic stronghold, is abbreviated Cal
USA is short for the United States of America

explanation.surface: A laid-back Democratic state propping up the nation against the president.
explanation.walkthrough: The anti-Trump state is California, the largest Democratic-voting state, shortened to CAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Casual clothes or manners are relaxed and not formal, so the two adjectives are direct synonyms.

clue.text: Gossip: "two Tory leaders caught in lie!"

indicators.note: leaders go at the front, so only opening letters are taken, here as many as the number says
something caught in a net is trapped inside it

blocks.note: a tale is a made-up story, a lie
the opening letter of the party name, taken twice

explanation.surface: A tabloid splash: a pair of Conservative leaders exposed telling untruths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two Tory leaders' reads as two party chiefs, but means the first letter of Tory, doubled.
explanation.definitionFit: Tattle is idle chatter about other people's affairs, the same as gossip used as a noun.

clue.text: Gents possibly seek out non-kosher butcher's

indicators.note: out and non-kosher both mean wrong or improper, so the letters are put wrongly

blocks.note: the Gents is a men's public toilet, a loo
taken as written

explanation.surface: Men going in search of a meat shop that is not kosher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butcher's' is cockney rhyming slang: butcher's hook rhymes with look. The Gents is the British name for a men's lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a butcher's means taking a look, and a look-see is a quick informal inspection, so both are slang nouns for a glance.

clue.text: (& 13ac. /2dn.) Pisspoor rap session singer – not right to boast about yourself

indicators.note: 'not' tells you to leave something out
something pisspoor is badly made, so the letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A rapper who blows their own trumpet gives a dreadful performance.
explanation.walkthrough: One R is removed from the three words before they are rearranged; the full answer runs across three grid entries.
explanation.definitionFit: To sing one's own praises is an idiom for bragging, here applied to oneself, so it matches self-promotion.

clue.text: Be a success screwing a frog

indicators.note: screwing twists something round, so the letters are turned into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A crude boast about scoring with an amphibian, or with a Frenchman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screwing' carries the usual Private Eye smut but is purely the signal to rearrange; 'frog' is also British slang for a French person.
explanation.definitionFit: To go far is an idiom for achieving a great deal in life or a career, so to succeed.

clue.text: End of Trump chaos engineered with IT? One needs to enter "nut"

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter
to engineer is to construct, so the letters are built into a new shape
to enter is to go inside something

blocks.note: the last letter of the name
taken as written
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: The Trump era's chaos ends with computer help, and someone labels the president a nut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' in quotation marks reads as calling someone mad, but it is the definition in its literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The pistachio is the green-kerneled edible seed of an Asian tree, eaten as a nut.

clue.text: Fool around near Gulf

indicators.note: one thing placed around another encloses it

blocks.note: an ass is a fool
by means near, as in standing by the door

explanation.surface: Someone messing about near the Persian Gulf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool around' reads as one phrasal verb, but the noun is the fool and 'around' is the wrapping signal; the Gulf is not a place but a chasm.
explanation.definitionFit: A gulf can be a deep chasm or vast gap, and an abyss is a bottomless pit, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Rolf turned over one grand in speedy extravagance

indicators.note: turning things over moves them about, mixing the order
'in' places the preceding group inside what follows

blocks.note: pacy means fast
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
G is short for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: Someone named Rolf blew a thousand pounds in a quick spending spree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned over' suggests a simple reversal, but ROLF backwards would be FLOR; only the last two letters swap.
explanation.definitionFit: Profligacy is recklessly wasteful spending, which is the same as extravagance in the sense of excess.

clue.text: (& 29ac.) Busybody who left front of car sticking out?

definitions.text: who left front of car sticking out?
definitions.note: a jokey description, read as a nose-y parker

blocks.note: first meaning: a person who pries into others' affairs

blocks.clueFragment: who left front of car sticking out?
blocks.note: second meaning: a driver who parked with the nose of the vehicle protruding

explanation.walkthrough: A nosy parker is the British idiom for a meddler; the second reading splits it as a parker whose car's nose juts out of the space.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosy parker is the everyday British phrase for someone who interferes and pries, exactly what a busybody does.

clue.text: see 28ac.
Strobes' unfinished, dodgy refresher course

indicators.note: something unfinished lacks its ending, so the final letter goes
dodgy means unreliable or crooked, so the letters are out of true

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Faulty flashing lights spoil a training course meant to refresh skills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refresher course' looks like retraining, but it is a course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A sorbet is served between dishes of a formal dinner to cleanse the palate, a refreshing dish in the menu.
